text: Wind is air on the move. It blows because [[@sun-what|the Sun]] heats Earth unevenly. Where the ground or sea gets warm, the air above it warms, spreads out and rises, leaving lower air pressure near the surface. Where it is cooler, air sinks and the pressure is higher.
Air always flows from high pressure towards low pressure, like water running downhill. That flow is the wind. The bigger the difference in pressure, the stronger it blows.

st.reveal: Land heats up faster than water in the sun. Warm air over the land rises, and cooler air from over the sea flows in to take its place. That is a sea breeze. At night, the land cools faster and the breeze often turns around.

myth: Trees make the wind by waving their branches.

Many young children think this, and the scientist Jean Piaget recorded it in the 1920s. It is the other way round. Wind is moving air, pushed by differences in air pressure, and it makes the trees sway.

sec.t:
Air has weight. The whole column of air above you presses down on everything, though you don't notice it. That push is called air [[pressure|pressure]].

When air is heated, its [[molecule|molecules]] move faster and spread out. Warm air is lighter than the same amount of cool air, so it rises, a bit like a hot-air balloon. Cooler, heavier air flows in underneath to replace it. A weather map with high and low pressure areas is really a map of where the wind will go.

Land heats up faster than water. On a sunny day at a beach in Goa or California, the sand gets hot by afternoon while the sea stays cooler. Air over the land rises, and cool air flows in from the sea. That is a sea breeze. At night the land cools faster, and a gentle breeze often blows the other way.

The [[@monsoon|monsoon]] works on a much bigger scale. In summer, the land of South Asia heats up much more than the Indian Ocean. Moist ocean air flows towards the land, bringing months of rain. In winter, the pattern reverses.

High above the ground, about 9 to 12 km up, narrow bands of very fast wind called [[@jet-streams|jet streams]] race around the planet from west to east. Pilots use them. A flight from the United States to Europe often takes less time than the return trip, because the plane rides the jet stream on the way.

Near the ground, the fastest winds come from [[@tornadoes|tornadoes]], but they are hard to measure. The [[@extreme-windiest|strongest gust recorded by an instrument]], outside a tornado, was 408 km/h during Cyclone Olivia in Australia in 1996. For decades before that, the [[@weather-records|record]] belonged to Mount Washington in New Hampshire, USA, with 372 km/h in 1934.

In 1805, the British naval officer Francis Beaufort devised a scale for sailors to describe wind by what it did to the sea and to a ship's sails. Later it was adapted for land: at force 3, leaves and twigs move; at force 6, umbrellas are hard to use; at force 10, trees are uprooted.

Today weather stations measure wind with spinning cups called anemometers. India's coasts and hills are also dotted with tall [[@wind-turbines|wind turbines]] that turn moving air into [[@electricity-made|electricity]]. India is one of the world's biggest producers of [[@renewable-energy|wind power]], and Tamil Nadu and Gujarat have some of its windiest sites.

text: A telescope is a light bucket. Its big [[@magnifying-glass|lens]] or curved mirror collects light from a distant object over a much larger area than your eye can. It then brings that light together into a sharp image, which you can look at through a small eyepiece lens or record with a camera.

The pupil of your eye is at most about 7 mm wide in the dark. Even a small [[@telescopes-make|backyard telescope]] with a 100 mm lens collects about 200 times more light. That is why a telescope shows thousands of stars where your eyes see a few, and turns smudges in the sky into [[@galaxies|galaxies]].

st.reveal: A wider mirror or lens collects more light, so the telescope can see fainter, more distant things and finer detail. Astronomers usually describe a telescope by its width, not its magnification.

myth: A telescope's main job is to make stars look bigger.
Stars are so far away that even the biggest telescopes show most of them as points. What a telescope mainly does is gather light, so faint things become visible.

sec.t:
The first known telescopes were made in the Netherlands around 1608. Spectacle makers found that two [[@lenses-glasses|lenses]] held in a line made faraway things look closer. In 1609 [[@galileo|Galileo]] heard about the idea and built his own. He pointed it at the sky and saw mountains on the Moon, moons around Jupiter and countless stars in the Milky Way.

{{story:lenses-glasses}}

A telescope that uses lenses is called a refractor, because the glass refracts, or bends, the light. The big front lens bends light to meet at a point. A smaller lens near your eye then spreads out that image so it fills your view.

The largest working refractor is at Yerkes Observatory in Wisconsin, USA, with a lens just over 1 m wide, finished in 1897. Lenses bigger than that sag under their own weight, because they can only be held at the edges.

In 1668 [[@newton-life|Isaac Newton]] built a different kind of telescope, using a curved mirror instead of a front lens. A mirror shaped like a shallow bowl reflects light to a point, just as a lens bends it. These are called reflectors.

Mirrors have big advantages. Light bounces off the front surface, so the glass behind it doesn't have to be perfectly clear. A mirror can be supported from behind, so it can be made much larger. Nearly every big research telescope today is a reflector.

India's largest is the Devasthal Optical Telescope in the hills of Uttarakhand, with a mirror 3.6 m across, working since 2016. In Chile, [[astronomer|astronomers]] are building the Extremely Large Telescope, whose main mirror, 39 m wide, is made of 798 hexagonal pieces. That is nearly twice the length of a cricket pitch, or about three school buses parked end to end.

Not all telescopes look at the light our eyes can see. Radio telescopes use giant metal dishes to collect [[@radio-waves|radio waves]] from space. Near [[@pune|Pune]], India's Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope uses 30 dishes, each 45 m across, spread out over about 25 km. Working together, they act like one enormous telescope.

Other telescopes sense [[infrared|infrared]], [[@x-rays|X-rays]] or [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light. Many of those signals are blocked by Earth's air, so the telescopes have to go to space. [[@hubble|Hubble]] and the [[@webb-telescope|James Webb Space Telescope]] are the most famous.

Light takes time to travel. When a telescope catches light from a [[galaxy|galaxy]] millions of [[lightyear|light-years]] away, that light set off millions of years ago. So the farther a telescope looks, the further back in time it sees.

That makes every big telescope a kind of time machine. The bigger the mirror, the fainter and older the light it can catch.

text: Yes. Wings are only one way into the air. A hot-air balloon floats because warm air is lighter than the cooler air around it, so the balloon rises like a bubble in water. A rocket blasts gas downward so hard that it shoots upward, and it works even in space, where there is no air at all.

Living things have their own tricks. Dandelion seeds drift for kilometres under a fluffy [[@parachutes|parachute]]. Baby spiders float away on threads of silk. And in Indian forests, some snakes, lizards and squirrels glide between trees. [[@gliders|Gliding]] is not quite flying, because they slowly lose height, but it gets them a long way.

sec.t:
On 21 November 1783, two men rose over Paris in a balloon made by the Montgolfier brothers. It was the first time people had been carried into the sky. Their balloon was filled with hot air from a fire burning below. Today, [[@weather-balloons|balloons filled with light helium gas]] carry weather instruments up to about 30 km high, and weather services around the world launch them every day.

Rockets work in a different way. They follow [[@newton-life|Isaac Newton]]'s rule that every push has an equal push back. As the engine forces gas out of the bottom, the gas pushes the rocket up. That is why [[@rockets-how|rockets]] can fly where balloons and wings cannot.

sec.h: Fish and frogs in the air
sec.t:
Some animals that glide live in water. [[@ocean-flying-fish|Flying fish]] burst out of the sea to escape hungry tuna and dolphins. They spread their large front fins like wings and can glide for more than 100 m. Some flick their tails on the surface as they come down, launching themselves into a second glide. Sailors crossing the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal often see them skimming over the waves.

In the [[@rainforests|rainforests]] of the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]] lives the Malabar gliding frog. It has big webbed feet that work like four small parachutes. When it leaps from a high branch, it spreads its toes and drifts down to a pond or a lower tree. It lays its eggs in a foam nest hanging over water, so the tadpoles drop straight in when they hatch.

A dandelion seed's fluffy top is mostly empty space. In 2018, scientists found that air flowing through the bristles makes a small swirling ring just above the seed. The ring helps keep it aloft. Other plants spin their seeds like [[@helicopters|helicopters]], as you can read in [[@seeds-fly|how seeds fly]].

The forests of India hold some skilled gliders. The ornate flying snake flattens its body and sails between trees. Small lizards called flying dragons, found in the Western Ghats, open flaps of skin along their sides. Giant flying squirrels can glide the length of a cricket ground and more. None of them flaps. They have all found a way to fall very slowly and in the right direction.

text: Sea snakes are snakes that live in the ocean. There are about 70 [[species|species]], found in warm, shallow seas from the east coast of Africa, across the Indian Ocean and around India, to Australia and the islands of the Pacific. There are none at all in the Atlantic.

They are [[@ocean-reptiles|reptiles]], related to cobras, and like cobras most are venomous. But their bodies have changed in clever ways for life in water. Their tails are flat like paddles. Their nostrils close with little flaps when they dive. And instead of slithering, they swim with smooth side-to-side waves of their bodies.

It has gills like a fish
It sucks bubbles of air from the water

st.reveal: Sea snakes are reptiles with lungs, so they must come to the surface to breathe. One lung stretches almost the length of the body, and some species can also take in a little oxygen through their skin, which helps them stay down for an hour or more.

sec.t:
[[biologist|Biologists]] split sea snakes into two groups. **True sea snakes** are fully at home in the ocean. They give birth to live babies in the water, and many would be clumsy and helpless if washed onto a beach. **Sea kraits** live a double life. They hunt at sea but crawl onto rocks and beaches to rest, digest their food and lay eggs. They are easy to spot, with bold black and blue-grey bands.

Most sea snakes hunt among [[@coral-reefs|coral reefs]], rocks and mangroves, poking their small heads into cracks for eels and fish. A few eat only fish eggs, and have tiny fangs and almost no [[venom|venom]].

Sea water is far too [[@why-sea-salty|salty]] to drink. Sea snakes have a [[gland|gland]] under the tongue that pushes out extra salt, but scientists found that many still get dangerously thirsty. In experiments, some refused salt water even after weeks without a drink, then gulped fresh water eagerly.

In the wild, they seem to rely on rain. After a heavy downpour, a thin layer of fresh water can float on top of the sea for a while, and sea snakes come up to drink it. In long dry spells they may go months without a proper drink.

sec.h: The snake that drifts across an ocean
sec.t: The yellow-bellied sea snake, black on top and bright yellow below, spends its life drifting in the open ocean, often near floating lines of seaweed and rubbish where small fish gather. It has the widest range of any snake. It is found from East Africa all the way to the Pacific coast of Mexico and Central America. During warm [[@el-nino|El Niño]] years, a few have even washed up on beaches in California.

Sea snake [[@snakes-venom|venom]] is powerful, but the snakes are usually calm. Divers often film them swimming past without trouble. Off India's coasts, most bites are from the beaked sea snake, and nearly all happen to fishermen sorting tangled nets, especially at night.

A sea snake on a beach should be left alone and reported to an adult, a lifeguard or the forest department. Along the coasts of Odisha, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Gujarat, sea snakes are a regular part of the catch that fishermen carefully throw back.

text: The platypus looks like it was put together from spare parts. It has a rubbery bill like a duck, a flat tail like a beaver, webbed feet like an otter and thick fur. It lays eggs like a bird. It is also one of very few venomous [[mammal|mammals]], and its family line is far older than the [[@mammals-rise|rise of most mammals]] after the dinosaurs.

None of this is a mix-up. The platypus belongs to the monotremes, the oldest surviving branch of mammals. Only the platypus and four kinds of echidna are left. Their ancestors split from other mammals well over 160 million years ago, while dinosaurs still ruled. They kept some ancient features, such as eggs, and [[evolve|evolved]] others, such as an electric bill.

sec.t:
In 1799, a dried platypus skin arrived in London from Australia. The naturalist George Shaw described it, but he admitted he could hardly believe his eyes. Some people suspected a prank, since sailors sometimes sewed animals together to sell as curiosities. Shaw reportedly looked for stitches around the bill.

That very skin is still kept at the Natural History Museum in London. It took scientists until 1884 to confirm that platypuses really lay eggs.

A mother platypus lays one to three eggs, each about the size of a grape, in a burrow in the riverbank. She curls around them for about 10 days. When the babies hatch, she has no nipples. Instead, milk oozes from patches of skin on her belly, and the babies lap it up from her fur.

Babies are tiny, about the size of a jelly bean, and stay hidden in the burrow for three to four months before they first swim out into the river.

Adults have no teeth either. Young platypuses have a few, but they fall out. Adults grind food between hard pads in their mouths, often scooping up gravel to help. And a platypus has no stomach. Its food goes straight from the gullet into the gut.

Male platypuses have a sharp spur on each back ankle, connected to a venom [[gland|gland]]. The venom is strongest in the breeding season, so scientists think males use it against each other. It can kill a dog. In people it causes pain so severe that ordinary painkillers barely help, sometimes for weeks.

That makes the platypus one of very few mammals with [[venom|venom]], alongside some shrews and the solenodon.

In 2020, scientists shone [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light on old museum specimens in the US and saw the brown fur glow blue-green. Nobody knows why. Platypuses are most active at dusk and night, so it might help them stay hidden, or it might mean nothing at all.

Platypuses are listed as near threatened, as droughts, dams and fires shrink their rivers. They live only in eastern [[@australia|Australia]], and their ten sex chromosomes, compared with our two, still puzzle geneticists. Some animals make their own light. Others, like the platypus, simply glow when light hits them, and the line between the two is stranger than it sounds.

text: A phad is a long painting on cloth from Rajasthan that tells the story of a folk hero. The most famous are about Pabuji, a warrior who is said to have brought camels to Rajasthan, and Devnarayan, a hero honoured by many herding families. Some phads stretch several metres, and the biggest Devnarayan scrolls are around 9 m, longer than three autorickshaws parked nose to tail.

A phad isn't made just to be looked at. At night, in a village, a pair of singer-priests called a *bhopa* and *bhopi* unroll it between two poles. They sing, dance and act out the hero's story, pointing at each scene with a lamp. A performance can last all night, and sometimes many nights.

st.reveal: Phad artists paint the hero and main gods much larger than other figures, and usually near the centre. Size shows importance, so you can spot the star of the story at a glance.

sec.h: A comic book from the past
sec.t:
A phad is crowded with people, horses, camels, palaces and battles. Scenes flow into each other without borders, a bit like a giant [[@comics-art|comic]] with no panels. The hero is painted biggest, usually near the middle. Less important people get smaller and smaller.

Faces are almost always shown from the side, with big almond-shaped eyes. The colours are bright and flat: yellow, orange, red, green, brown and blue, with bold black outlines. There is little shading, so the figures look like they are cut from coloured paper.

For generations, phads were painted mainly by the Joshi family of Bhilwara and Shahpura. The bhopas, who were mostly from herding communities, ordered them and paid with money or grain. The painter started work on an auspicious day and often finished by painting the hero's eyes. That moment brought the phad to life.

In the 20th century, Shree Lal Joshi became famous for phad painting and trained many students, including people outside his family. He received the Padma Shri, one of India's highest civilian honours, in 2006. Members of the family now teach workshops, and women paint phads too.

For the people who watch, a phad is a moving temple. The gods painted on it are believed to be present when it is unrolled. Families invite the bhopas when someone is ill, when animals are sick, or to give thanks.

The bhopa plays the *ravanhattha*, a bowed string instrument made with a coconut shell, said to be one of the oldest bowed instruments in India. The songs are long, in a local language, with spoken parts and jokes.

When a phad becomes too worn to use, it is retired with care. It may be "cooled" by being placed in water, often at the holy lake of [[@india-wonder-pushkar|Pushkar]].

Today phad painters also paint the Ramayana, the life of the Buddha, stories of Gandhi, and even messages about clean water or girls' education. Tourists buy small phads as souvenirs.

Fewer bhopas perform now, because television and phones fill village evenings. But some still unroll their scrolls at fairs. And Pabuji's tale has a memorable link to animals: in the story he brings the first [[@camels|camels]] to Rajasthan, a gift for his niece's wedding.

text: Child labour means work that is harmful for children or stops them going to school. It isn't the same as helping at home, running an errand or doing a few hours of light work that suits your age.

It is wrong because childhood is when bodies grow and brains learn fastest. A child carrying bricks or breathing dust in a workshop can be injured for life. A child who leaves school at ten may never learn to read well, and will probably earn less as an adult. Their own children are then more likely to work too, so the cycle repeats. Almost every country now bans the worst kinds of child work.

sec.t:
In the United States, Lewis Hine worked for the National Child Labor Committee from 1908. He sometimes pretended to be a salesman or a fire inspector to get inside mills, mines and canneries. He photographed children at spinning machines and boys covered in coal dust, and wrote down their names and ages.

His photos, now kept by the Library of Congress, shocked many Americans. They helped build support for the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, which set minimum ages for work across the country. [[@photography-history|Photography]] had shown people what words alone had not.

India's Constitution bans children under 14 from working in factories, mines and other dangerous jobs. Since 2016, the law has banned nearly all work for children under 14, apart from helping a family business after school hours. Teenagers aged 14 to 18 cannot do hazardous work.

Since 2010, the right to education has made school free and compulsory for children aged 6 to 14. Free school lunches through the [[@mid-day-meal|mid-day meal]] scheme have given poor families another reason to send children to class. Kailash Satyarthi's group, Bachpan Bachao Andolan, has rescued many thousands of children from workshops and factories since 1980. He shared the [[@nobel-peace|Nobel Peace Prize]] in 2014.

Most child labour today is not in factories but on farms, in homes and in small workshops. It usually comes from poverty. If a family can't afford food, a child's small wage can feel like the only choice. Debt, illness in the family, a disaster or a school too far away make it more likely.

That is why the solutions are often about families as much as children. Fair wages for parents, schools close to home, free meals and good inspections all help. The number of child labourers fell by tens of millions between 2000 and 2020. Even so, the ILO and UNICEF estimated about 138 million in 2024, and every 12 June the world marks a day against child labour to keep the problem in view. Each child back in a classroom is a cycle broken.

text: Congress is the part of the US government that makes [[federal|federal]] laws, the laws for the whole country. It has two chambers. The House of Representatives has 435 voting members, with more seats for states that have more people. The Senate has 100 members, two from each of the 50 states.

A bill must pass both chambers in exactly the same words. Then it goes to the President, who can sign it into law or reject it with a [[veto|veto]]. The rules come from Article I of the [[@us-constitution|US Constitution]], written in 1787.

Congress writes and passes federal laws. The President can sign a bill or veto it, but Congress can override a veto if two-thirds of both chambers vote to do so.

sec.h: A deal between big and small
sec.t:
When the Constitution was being written, small states feared that big states would outvote them every time. Big states thought it unfair for a tiny state to have the same say as a huge one. The compromise, often called the Great Compromise, gave Congress two chambers. The House counts people. The Senate counts states.

That is why Wyoming, with about 6 lakh people, and California, with nearly 4 crore, each have two senators. In the House, California has 52 representatives and Wyoming has one. Six states have only one representative each.

House seats are shared out by population, so the country must know how many people live in each state. Every ten years, the US carries out a [[@census|census]], a count of every person. After each one, states that have grown may gain seats, and states that have shrunk may lose them. Texas and Florida gained seats after the 2020 count.

{{story:census}}

Members of the House face voters every two years, so they must stay close to what people at home think. Bills about raising money through taxes must start in the House. The House can also impeach, or formally accuse, a president or a judge of serious wrongdoing.

Senators serve six years, and only a third of the seats are up for election at a time. The Senate holds the trial if someone is impeached. It also approves [[treaty|treaties]] with other countries and confirms the people a president picks for top jobs, including Supreme Court [[@courts-judges|judges]]. The Vice President presides over the Senate and can cast a vote only to break a tie.

Congress meets in the Capitol building in [[@washington-dc|Washington, D.C.]], under a white dome topped by a bronze statue called Freedom. The House sits in the south wing and the Senate in the north. People living in Washington, D.C., which is not a state, elect a delegate to the House who can speak but cannot vote on final bills.

Much of the real work happens away from the big chambers, in committees. Small groups of members study bills on subjects like farming, defence or education. They hold hearings, question experts and rewrite the wording. Most bills are quietly dropped at this stage and never reach a full vote. Visitors can watch debates from public galleries, and both chambers are shown live on television.

Getting the House, the Senate and the President to agree is hard, and most bills never become law. The writers of the Constitution designed it that way, so no single group could grab too much power quickly. Critics say it can make Congress slow to act even when most people want change. In India the job is shared differently, as you can see in [[@parliament-india|How does India's Parliament work?]], where the government comes from the majority in the elected house.

text: Socrates was a philosopher who lived in Athens, in [[@ancient-greece|ancient Greece]], about 2,400 years ago. He spent his days in the marketplace asking people questions about big ideas: What is justice? What is courage? How should a good person live?

He never wrote anything down and never ran a school. Instead, he talked. His questions often showed that important, confident people did not understand things as well as they thought. Many young Athenians loved him for it, and many powerful ones disliked him. In 399 BCE he was put on trial, found guilty and sentenced to death. His student Plato wrote down his conversations, and through them Socrates became one of the most famous thinkers in history.

options.t: By asking people questions until they saw the holes in their own ideas
By writing long books for his students to memorise
By giving speeches in a big school he founded

st.reveal: Socrates walked around the marketplace of Athens chatting with anyone who would talk. He asked simple questions like "What is courage?" and kept asking until people saw that their answers didn't hold up. This style is now called the Socratic method.

n.certNote: Socrates left no writings. Almost everything we know comes from his students, especially Plato and Xenophon, and from a comic play that mocked him. Historians debate how much of "Socrates" in Plato's books is the real man and how much is Plato's own ideas.

sec.t:
Socrates was born around 470 BCE. Ancient writers say his father was a stonemason and his mother a midwife. He fought as a foot soldier in Athens' wars and was said to be very brave and very tough, walking barefoot even in winter.

He was famous for not caring about money or fine clothes. He was also, according to his friends, rather ugly, with a snub nose and bulging eyes. That made his charm in conversation even more surprising.

A friend of Socrates once asked the famous oracle at Delphi, a temple where people went to ask the gods questions, whether anyone was wiser than Socrates. The answer came back: no one.

Socrates was puzzled, because he didn't think he was wise. So he went around questioning politicians, poets and craftsmen. He found that they believed they knew things they didn't. He decided he was wiser only in one way: he knew how little he knew.

In 399 BCE, Socrates was accused of not respecting the city's gods and of corrupting the young. He was tried in front of a jury of about 500 ordinary citizens, as was normal in [[@democracy-athens|Athens]]. Some Athenians were angry because a few of his former followers had sided with the city's enemies or with cruel rulers.

In Plato's account, Socrates didn't beg for mercy. He said that the unexamined life is not worth living. A majority found him guilty and voted for death. His friends offered to help him escape, but he refused, saying he would obey the laws of the city.

Socrates was given a drink made from a poisonous plant called hemlock. Plato's book Phaedo describes his last day, spent calmly talking with friends about whether the soul lives on after death.

In 1787, the French artist Jacques-Louis David painted the scene, with Socrates reaching for the cup while pointing upwards and still talking. The painting hangs in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. People still argue about the trial. Some see it as a warning about how even a [[democracy|democracy]] can punish someone for asking awkward questions, a debate that connects to [[@free-speech|free speech]] today.

Socrates was born about ten years after [[@confucius|Confucius]] died in China, and lived in roughly the same era as the Buddha in India. Like them, he taught by talking, and his students wrote his ideas down. Plato went on to teach Aristotle, who later taught Alexander the Great, so the questions asked in an Athenian marketplace travelled far.

text: Most historians think chess grew from a game called *chaturanga*, played in India around the 6th century CE. *Chaturanga* means "four parts", the four parts of an army: foot soldiers, horses, elephants and chariots. They became today's pawns, knights, bishops and rooks.

It was played on an 8 by 8 board, the same size as today's. A king sat at the centre of each army, with a counsellor beside him. The goal was the one chess players still chase: trap the enemy king so that it cannot escape.

st.reveal: Doubling 63 times gives over 9 quintillion grains on the last square alone. That is hundreds of years' worth of all the rice the world grows.

In chaturanga and the Persian game, the piece beside the king was a counsellor that moved just one square diagonally. Players in Europe turned it into the powerful queen around the end of the 1400s.

sec.t:
Traders and travellers carried the game along the [[@trade-routes|trade routes]] to Persia, where it was called *shatranj*. From there it spread to the Arab world and Europe. Our word "checkmate" comes from the Persian *shah mat*: "the king is helpless."

The Persian poet Ferdowsi, writing about a thousand years ago in the *Shahnameh*, told a story of how chess arrived. An Indian king sent the game to the Persian court as a puzzle, daring the wise men to work out its rules. In the story, a minister solved it and sent back a game of his own, an ancestor of backgammon. It is a legend, but it shows that Persians themselves remembered chess as a gift from India.

Chaturanga copied the armies of ancient India. Kings went to war with four kinds of troops: foot soldiers, cavalry on horses, war elephants and chariots. Old [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] texts call such an army *chaturangini*, meaning one with four limbs.

On the board, the elephant became the bishop in English, though in Hindi the bishop is still often called *oont*, the camel, and the rook is *haathi*, the elephant. Many Indian players also call the queen *wazir*, the minister. The names have shifted as the game travelled, but the army is still there.

sec.h: How the queen got her power
sec.t:
For about a thousand years, the counsellor next to the king was one of the weakest pieces on the board. Around 1475, players in [[@spain|Spain]] gave it the power to sweep across the board in any direction, and renamed it the queen. Bishops gained long diagonal moves at about the same time.

Games suddenly became faster and fiercer. Some people called the new version "mad queen chess". Within a few decades it had spread across Europe, and the rules have barely changed since.

In 1997, an IBM computer called Deep Blue beat world champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match. Today, chess programs are far stronger than any human, and players use them to train.

India has produced many great players. [[@viswanathan-anand|Viswanathan Anand]] became India's first [[grandmaster|grandmaster]] in 1988 and later won the world championship several times. In 2024, 18-year-old D. Gukesh became the youngest undisputed world champion in history, one of a long line of [[@chess-champions|India's chess champions]]. The game came home, and India's players are now among the best on the board.

text: Medicines don't actually know where to go. When you swallow a tablet, it [[dissolve|dissolves]], gets absorbed into your blood and is carried all around your body. It only has an effect in places where it meets the right target.

Most targets are special [[molecule|molecules]] on or inside cells, such as [[receptor|receptors]] or [[enzyme|enzymes]]. A medicine's shape lets it fit onto its target like a key into a lock. It might block a lock to stop a signal, like a painkiller blocking a pain chemical, or turn a lock to start one. Because the same targets can exist in many parts of the body, medicines sometimes have side effects in places you didn't intend.

st.reveal: James Lind split 12 sick sailors into pairs and tried six treatments. The pair given citrus fruit recovered fastest. Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C, though nobody knew about vitamins then. Lind's careful comparison is often called one of the first controlled medical trials.

sec.t:
A tablet first breaks apart in your stomach. Most medicines are absorbed through the walls of the small intestine into the blood. That blood flows first to the [[@liver|liver]], which breaks down some of the medicine before it reaches the rest of the body. Doctors take this into account when they choose a dose.

From there, the heart pumps the medicine everywhere. Over hours, the liver and kidneys gradually remove it, which is why many medicines must be taken several times a day. Some medicines skip this route. Injections go straight into the blood or muscle, inhalers go into the lungs, and creams work on the skin.

Doctors need proof that a medicine really works. In 1747, the Scottish naval doctor James Lind tested six treatments on 12 sailors with scurvy. Only the pair given oranges and lemons recovered quickly. His fair comparison is often called one of the first controlled trials.

Today, new medicines go through years of testing. They're tried in the lab, then in small groups of volunteers, then in larger trials where some patients get the real medicine and others get a dummy pill. Neither patients nor doctors know who got which, so their hopes can't affect the results. The [[@placebo|placebo]] effect, where people feel better from a dummy pill, is surprisingly strong, which is exactly why these checks matter.

Once a medicine's [[@patents|patent]] expires, other companies can make cheaper copies called generics. India is one of the world's biggest makers of generic medicines and [[vaccine|vaccines]]. It supplies many countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America, and a large share of the generic tablets used in the USA. This has helped bring the price of many important medicines, including HIV treatments, down sharply.

Medicines are powerful, which is why they need care. Never take medicine on your own or share someone else's prescription. The 16th-century Swiss doctor Paracelsus is remembered for a famous idea: the dose makes the poison. Even water is harmful in huge amounts, and the right medicine at the wrong dose can be dangerous. Always let a trusted adult or doctor decide what you take and how much.

text: Wi-Fi lets phones, laptops and other devices connect to the internet without wires, using radio waves.

At the heart of it is a box called a router. It connects to the internet through a cable. The router turns data from the internet into radio signals and sends them out through the air. Your device picks up those signals with a tiny antenna and turns them back into data. When you send something, like a message, the same thing happens in reverse.
It all happens millions of times a second, so web pages and videos appear almost instantly.

st.reveal: Wi-Fi signals get weaker with distance, and thick walls, metal, mirrors and even water tanks absorb or block them. Moving the router to a central, high spot often helps the whole house.

sec.t:
[[@radio-waves|Radio waves]] are a kind of light our eyes can't see. Like ripples on a pond, they have a [[frequency|frequency]], which means how many waves pass a point each second. Wi-Fi mostly uses waves at 2.4 gigahertz (2.4 billion waves a second) and 5 gigahertz. Newer routers also use 6 gigahertz.

To carry information, the router changes the waves in tiny, precise ways, shifting their strength and timing. Each change stands for a group of 0s and 1s, the [[binary|binary]] language of computers. Your device reads the changes and rebuilds the data.

The 2.4 gigahertz band reaches further and passes walls better. The higher bands carry more data but fade faster.

In a busy home, many devices share one router. A phone streams a cricket match, a laptop joins a video call, a games console downloads an update. They can't all talk at once on the same channel, or their signals would jam.

So Wi-Fi uses rules for taking turns. Each device listens first, and only sends when the air is clear. Modern routers can also talk to several devices at once by splitting their channel into smaller pieces. Large buildings like [[@airports|airports]] and stations use many routers so no single one gets overloaded.

In 1997, engineers agreed on a shared set of rules for wireless networks, called IEEE 802.11. Because every company followed the same rules, devices from different makers could talk to each other.

A key problem was [[@echoes|echoes]]. Indoors, radio waves bounce off walls and furniture and arrive at slightly different times, blurring the signal. A team at CSIRO, [[@australia|Australia]]'s national science agency, led by the radio [[astronomer|astronomer]] John O'Sullivan, developed ways to deal with this, based partly on techniques from studying signals from space. In 1999, a group of companies gave the technology a catchier name: Wi-Fi.

Wi-Fi now connects billions of devices, from phones to smart TVs to doorbells. Many cities, cafes, airports and libraries offer free Wi-Fi. In 2016, [[@mumbai|Mumbai]] Central became one of the first [[@indian-railways|Indian railway]] stations to offer free high-speed Wi-Fi, and hundreds of stations followed.

Because Wi-Fi travels through the air, anyone nearby can try to listen. That's why home networks use [[@passwords|passwords]] and [[encryption|encryption]], which scrambles data so only the right devices can read it. On public Wi-Fi, it's wise to avoid entering private information unless the website is secure.

text: Goa was ruled by Portugal for about 450 years, from 1510 to 1961. When the rest of India became independent from Britain in 1947, Portugal refused to leave. It claimed Goa was a part of Portugal itself, not a colony.

For fourteen years, Goans and other Indians protested, and India tried to negotiate. Portugal would not move. Finally, on 18 December 1961, the Indian Army, Navy and Air Force entered Goa, Daman and Diu in Operation Vijay. The Portuguese Governor-General surrendered the next day. Goa became part of India, and in 1987 it became a full state.

Several areas stayed under foreign rule. Goa, Daman and Diu remained Portuguese until 1961, and French territories such as Puducherry were handed over in stages between 1950 and 1962.

sec.t:
In 1498 the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama reached Calicut, in Kerala, opening a sea route from Europe to India. Portugal wanted control of the trade in [[@cardamom-pepper|pepper]] and other [[@spices|spices]], which sold for huge profits in Europe.

In 1510, the commander Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from the [[@india-wonder-gol-gumbaz|Sultan of Bijapur]]. It became the capital of Portugal's [[empire|empire]] in Asia. Old Goa grew into a grand city of churches, including the Basilica of Bom Jesus, which holds the remains of the missionary Francis Xavier. Portuguese rule left a deep mark on Goa's languages, music, [[architecture|architecture]] and [[@goan-food|food]].

After 1947, Prime Minister [[@nehru|Nehru]] hoped Portugal would leave peacefully, as France was beginning to do with its Indian [[territory|territories]]. Portugal's dictator, António de Oliveira Salazar, refused to even discuss it.

In 1954, volunteers took control of the tiny Portuguese [[enclave|enclaves]] of Dadra and Nagar Haveli. In 1955, thousands of unarmed satyagrahis, inspired by Gandhi's methods, marched into Goa from different points. Portuguese police fired on them, and some were killed while many more were injured or arrested. People across India were outraged. India cut diplomatic ties with Portugal soon after.

By 1961, India's patience had run out. Around the world, colonies in Africa and Asia were winning freedom, part of the wave of [[@decolonisation|decolonisation]], and Indian leaders felt Goa could wait no longer.

On the night of 17–18 December, Indian forces crossed into Goa from several directions, while the navy moved against Diu and Anjediva island. The Portuguese had only a few thousand troops. On 19 December, Governor-General Manuel António Vassalo e Silva surrendered, ignoring orders from Lisbon to fight to the last. Goans celebrate 19 December as Liberation Day.

Some countries, including the United States and Britain, criticised India at the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] for using force. A resolution against India was blocked by the Soviet Union. Portugal finally recognised Indian rule over Goa in 1974, after its own revolution ended the dictatorship.

In January 1967, Goans voted in an opinion poll on whether to join Maharashtra. A majority chose to remain separate. In 1987 Goa became India's 25th state, and Konkani was made its official language.

text: The Voynich [[manuscript|manuscript]] is a small, thick book about the size of a school notebook. Its pages are packed with flowing handwriting in an alphabet found nowhere else on Earth. Around the words are drawings of plants that don't quite match any real plant, circles of stars, and tiny people bathing in green pools connected by strange tubes.

Scientists have dated its pages to the early 1400s. That is roughly when the [[@vijayanagara|Vijayanagara]] [[empire|empire]] ruled much of south India. Since 1969 it has lived at Yale University in the USA, catalogued as MS 408. Anyone can look at every page online. Nobody can read a single word.

st.reveal: Carbon dating at the University of Arizona showed the animal-skin pages were made between about 1404 and 1438. That ruled out the idea that Voynich himself forged it, though the ink could in theory have been added later.

sec.h: A book with a strange family tree
sec.t:
The book is named after Wilfrid Voynich, a Polish-born bookseller who bought it in Italy in 1912. Tucked inside was a letter from 1665 or 1666. It claimed that Emperor Rudolf II of Bohemia, a ruler who loved oddities, had paid 600 gold coins for it. If that is true, it was a fortune for a book nobody could understand.

Before that, the trail goes cold. We don't know who wrote it, where, or why.

Experts sort the pages into sections by their pictures. There are about 240 pages left, and some fold out to several times the normal size.

- **Plants:** over 100 drawings, most of them unidentified.
- **Stars and [[zodiac|zodiac]]:** circular charts with suns, moons and star signs.
- **Bathing:** small figures in pools and pipes.
- **Medicine:** jars, roots and leaves, a bit like a pharmacy guide.
- **Text only:** short paragraphs marked with little stars.

The writing runs smoothly, with no crossings-out. Whoever wrote it seems to have known exactly what they were putting down.

{{story:codes-enigma}}

After the Second World War, William Friedman, one of America's greatest code experts, set up a team to study it. These were people who had cracked enemy [[cipher|ciphers]]. They got nowhere.

Here is the odd part. The text behaves a lot like real language. Some words appear very often and most appear rarely, which is how English, Hindi and every other language work. But some words repeat two or three times in a row, which real languages almost never do. And a few "words" appear only in certain sections, as if each part has its own vocabulary.

Computers have since counted every character. That gives people a lot to argue about, but no answers.

**It's a real language in an invented [[script|script]].** Someone may have written a known language, such as a [[dialect|dialect]] of German or Italian, in a home-made alphabet. Then the challenge is matching the shapes to sounds.

**It's a code.** The words might be scrambled using a system, like the ones in [[@cryptography-maths|cryptography]]. If so, it is a very unusual one.

**It's a hoax.** In 2004 a British computer scientist, Gordon Rugg, showed that a simple card with holes could churn out text with some Voynich-like patterns. Others reply that a fake from the 1400s would have taken months of careful work, all for a joke.

Every claim to have solved it fails the same test. A real solution should let you read a page you haven't seen yet. So far, none does.

The Voynich manuscript is not the only unreadable writing in the world. The [[@indus-script|Indus script]], carved on seals more than 4,000 years ago, also waits for its key. The difference is that the Indus people left only short lines. The Voynich author left an entire book, and still told us nothing.

text: Spies have always tried to find out what the other side is planning, without being caught. For most of history, they did it with eyes, ears and memory. They counted soldiers and ships, listened to gossip in markets, read stolen letters and sent messages in code or invisible ink.

As technology changed, so did spying. Pigeons carried notes across enemy lines. Radios sent secret messages across Europe. Codebreakers used early computing machines to read enemy signals. But the basic job stayed the same: learn secrets, pass them on, and stay hidden.

Most spying was slow and ordinary work, like counting ships, copying letters, listening in markets and passing notes. Many of the most useful spies were shopkeepers, servants, farmers and radio operators whom nobody suspected.

sec.t:
More than 2,000 years ago in India, the *Arthashastra*, a book on running a kingdom linked to [[@chanakya|Chanakya]], adviser to the Mauryan emperor Chandragupta, described spies in great detail. Its spies could pose as monks, students, merchants, farmers or wandering performers.

The book advised kings to have spies watch enemies, foreign courts and even their own ministers. It suggested checking reports from several spies, so no single liar could fool the king. Similar advice appears in China's *Art of War*, traditionally credited to Sun Tzu, which says knowing the enemy wins battles.

During the American Revolution, George Washington needed to know what the British army was doing in New York. From 1778, a group called the Culper Ring sent him reports. Its members included a farmer, a tavern keeper and a shopkeeper.

They used a code book with numbers for important words. Washington was 711. They wrote with an invisible "sympathetic stain". One story says Anna Strong, a member, signalled where to meet by hanging a black petticoat and a number of handkerchiefs on her washing line. Their reports helped warn of British plans.

During the American Civil War, [[@harriet-tubman|Harriet Tubman]], who had escaped slavery, worked as a scout and spy for the Union Army. In 1863 she helped lead the Combahee River Raid in South Carolina, which freed more than 700 enslaved people. Her knowledge of hidden paths and her network of contacts made it possible.

{{story:codes-enigma}}

In the Second World War, spying became huge. Noor Inayat Khan, a [[descendant|descendant]] of Tipu Sultan, was born in Moscow and grew up in Paris and London. In 1943 she became a secret radio operator for Britain in Nazi-occupied Paris. For months she moved from flat to flat, sending messages while the Gestapo hunted her. She was captured and killed in 1944, and received the George Cross for her bravery.

At Bletchley Park in England, thousands of codebreakers worked to read German messages scrambled by the [[@codes-enigma|Enigma]] machine. Pigeons carried messages too, and some won medals.

Spying also works in reverse. Armies try to trick the other side's spies. In 1944 and 1945, a secret US unit nicknamed the Ghost Army used inflatable rubber tanks, recorded truck sounds and fake radio messages. The aim was to make the Germans think a big army was somewhere it was not. A rubber tank could be pumped up in minutes and carried by a few soldiers, a cousin of the party [[@made-balloons|balloon]].

In [[medieval|medieval]] Japan, *shinobi* did secret scouting and spying for warlords. Later stories turned them into the black-clad [[@ninjas|ninjas]] of films, who are far more magical than the real thing ever was.

text: Everest Base Camp is a seasonal tent village high in the Himalaya, where climbers prepare to scale the world's highest mountain. There are two. The busier South Base Camp in Nepal sits at about 5,364 metres on the Khumbu Glacier. The North Base Camp in Tibet, reached by road, is at about 5,150 metres.

In spring, hundreds of colourful tents spread across the rocky ice. It is cold, windy and dusty, with thin air that leaves visitors puffing after a few steps. Yet it also has kitchens, medical tents, satellite internet and prayer flags snapping in the wind. For tens of thousands of trekkers every year, simply reaching base camp is the adventure.

Because the trail closes on certain days

st.reveal: Climbing too fast can cause altitude sickness, with headaches, sickness and, rarely, dangerous swelling of the brain or lungs. Spending extra nights at the same height lets the body make more red blood cells and adjust. Trekkers follow the rule "climb high, sleep low".

sec.t:
Most people reach the Nepal side on foot. The trip usually starts with a short flight to Lukla, a village with a famously short, sloping runway on a mountainside. From there, it takes about eight or nine days to walk up, with rest days built in.

The trail follows the Dudh Kosi river valley through pine forests and over swaying suspension bridges. It passes through Namche Bazaar, a Sherpa town built in a horseshoe on a hillside, with bakeries, gear shops and a weekly market. Higher up, trees disappear, and so do most plants. Yaks and porters carry supplies, as there are no roads. Some porters carry loads heavier than a large suitcase on their backs, held by a strap across the forehead.

At base camp, each breath holds roughly half the oxygen it would at sea level. Visitors get headaches, sleep badly and lose their appetite. That is why treks build in rest days, so the body can adjust to the [[@altitude|altitude]].

Climbers heading for the top spend weeks going up and down between higher camps to get used to it. Above base camp lies the Khumbu Icefall, a jumbled maze of ice blocks and deep cracks. Sherpa specialists called "icefall doctors" fix ladders and ropes across it every season.

Many of the people who make Everest climbs possible are Sherpas, a mountain people of eastern Nepal whose ancestors came from Tibet. Their bodies are well suited to high altitude, and their skills on the mountain are essential.

In 1953, Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa who had grown up in the Khumbu region, reached the [[@everest-first|summit]] with Edmund Hillary of New Zealand. Today Sherpa guides hold many Everest records, and several have climbed it more than 20 times.

Base camp now faces big problems. Crowds leave rubbish and human waste that does not rot in the cold. Nepal now asks climbers to bring rubbish back down, and clean-up teams carry tonnes of waste off the mountain each year.

The [[glacier|glacier]] itself is thinning as the [[climate|climate]] warms, and Nepal's government has talked about moving base camp lower in future. The area is part of Sagarmatha National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979. Sagarmatha is the Nepali name for Everest. In Tibet, it is called Chomolungma.

text: Sri Lanka is an island nation shaped like a teardrop, just off the southern tip of India. It is famous for its tea, spices, beaches, elephants and ancient cities, and for its cricket.

The island packs a lot into a small space. It has misty hills covered in tea gardens, dry plains with huge old [[reservoir|reservoirs]], rainforest, and golden beaches all around. Most people are Sinhala, and most of them are Buddhist. There are also large Tamil, Muslim and Christian communities, and the country uses Sinhala and Tamil as official languages, with English widely spoken.

sec.t:
In the 5th century CE, a king called Kashyapa built a palace on top of Sigiriya, a rock that rises about 180 m out of the forest. Visitors climbed through the open jaws of a giant stone lion, whose huge paws still guard the stairway.

Halfway up, painted women still gaze out from a sheltered rock face. A polished wall nearby, called the Mirror Wall, is covered in poems scratched by visitors over 1,000 years ago, among the oldest [[@oddity-ancient-graffiti|graffiti]] anywhere. Further north, the ancient cities of Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa have giant [[stupa|stupas]] and reservoirs, called tanks, that still water rice fields.

In Anuradhapura grows the Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi, a sacred fig tree. According to tradition, Sanghamitta, a daughter of the emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]], brought a cutting of the tree under which the [[@buddha|Buddha]] found enlightenment at [[@bihar-history|Bodh Gaya]]. It was planted in 288 BCE.

Monks and pilgrims have tended it for over 2,000 years, propping up its heavy branches with golden supports. Many Hindus, too, link Sri Lanka with the island of Lanka in the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]], and pilgrims visit sites connected with the story.

Sri Lanka has many wild Asian elephants for its size. Each year in the dry season, hundreds gather to graze around the shrinking Minneriya reservoir, an event known as "the Gathering". Off the southern coast, near Mirissa, boats take visitors to see [[@blue-whale|blue whales]], the largest animals ever to live.

Spices drew traders here for centuries. Arab, Portuguese, Dutch and British ships came for cinnamon, which grows wild in the island's forests. In 1996, Sri Lanka won the men's Cricket World Cup, beating Australia in the final in Lahore.

From 1983 to 2009, Sri Lanka suffered a long civil war between the government and the Tamil Tigers, an armed group fighting for a separate Tamil state. Tens of thousands of people died, many of them civilians, and families on all sides still carry its memory. In 2004 the Indian Ocean [[tsunami|tsunami]] struck its eastern and southern coasts.

In 2022, the country ran short of money for fuel, food and medicine, and protests forced the president to resign. Sri Lanka has been slowly rebuilding since.

text: The Guru Granth Sahib is the holy [[scripture|scripture]] of Sikhism. Sikhs believe it is the living Guru, the spiritual teacher who guides them. It is a book of hymns: poems written to be sung, praising one God and describing how to live a good, honest and humble life.

It is written in the Gurmukhi script and has 1,430 pages. Most of the hymns are by the Sikh Gurus, starting with [[@guru-nanak|Guru Nanak]], who founded the faith about 500 years ago in Punjab. It also includes poems by Hindu and Muslim saints whose ideas the Gurus shared.

st.reveal: Most of the book is divided into sections by raga, the musical mode used to sing the hymns. Within each raga section, hymns are grouped by author and form. The book is meant to be sung as much as read.

sec.t:
Guru Nanak and the Gurus who came after him composed hymns and sang them with their followers. These were written down and passed on. Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, gathered them into one book with the help of a scholar named Bhai Gurdas. In 1604, this first version, called the Adi Granth ("the first book"), was placed in the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, now known as the [[@golden-temple|Golden Temple]].

The tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, later added the hymns of his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur. In 1708, shortly before he died, Guru Gobind Singh declared that there would be no more human Gurus. From then on, the scripture itself would be the Guru, and it became the Guru Granth Sahib.

The Gurus included poems by saints called Bhagats. Among them are [[@mirabai-kabir|Kabir]], a weaver from Varanasi, and Ravidas, a leather worker. There is Namdev, a tailor-poet from Maharashtra, and Sheikh Farid, a Sufi Muslim from Punjab who lived about 300 years before Guru Nanak.

For Sikhs, this shows a central belief: that truth and devotion are not owned by any one group. People of very different faiths and backgrounds, some from communities that were looked down on in their time, share the same pages.

In a gurdwara, the Sikh place of worship, the Guru Granth Sahib rests on a raised platform under a [[canopy|canopy]], wrapped in cloth when not being read. An attendant often waves a whisk called a chaur over it, a sign of respect once shown to kings. At night, in many gurdwaras, it is carried to a separate room to rest, and it is brought back in the morning.

Each morning the book is opened at a random page, and a hymn from the top of the left-hand page is read aloud. This is called the *hukamnama*, the order or guidance for the day. The hukamnama from the Golden Temple is now shared online every day, so Sikhs in Toronto, London or California can read the same hymn as worshippers in Amritsar.

Visitors of any faith are welcome. They cover their heads, take off their shoes and sit on the floor. On special occasions, a team of readers takes turns to read the whole book aloud without stopping, which takes about 48 hours. This is called an Akhand Path. Afterwards, everyone may share a free community meal called langar, cooked and served by volunteers.

text: India has produced many famous writers in English. Some of the best known are R. K. Narayan, who wrote the Malgudi stories, and Ruskin Bond, who writes about the Himalayan hills. Salman Rushdie, Arundhati Roy, Vikram Seth and Amitav Ghosh are read across the world.

English came with the British, who ruled much of India for nearly two hundred years. At first it was the language of offices and courts. Then Indians began to write poems and novels in it. They brought in Indian [[rhythm|rhythms]], food, festivals and jokes. Today Indian English is one of the liveliest forms of the language anywhere.

sec.t:
Toru Dutt, from a Bengali family in Kolkata, wrote poems in English and French in the 1870s, and died at only 21. [[@sarojini-naidu|Sarojini Naidu]] published poems in the early 1900s before becoming a freedom fighter. [[@tagore|Rabindranath Tagore]] wrote mostly in Bengali, but his own English version of *Gitanjali* helped win him the Nobel Prize in 1913.

In the 1930s three novelists set the pattern. Mulk Raj Anand wrote *Untouchable* about a young sweeper. Raja Rao wrote *Kanthapura* about a village joining Gandhi's movement. And R. K. Narayan invented Malgudi. The English writer Graham Greene liked Narayan's first [[manuscript|manuscript]] and helped him find a publisher in London in 1935.

In 1981 Salman Rushdie's *Midnight's Children* won the [[@booker-prize|Booker Prize]]. Its hero is born at the exact moment of India's independence, and his life is tangled with the country's. Vikram Seth's *A Suitable Boy* (1993) runs to about 1,350 pages and is one of the longest single novels in English. Arundhati Roy's *The God of Small Things* won the Booker in 1997.

Amitav Ghosh writes about the Sundarbans, the opium trade and [[climate|climate]] change. In 2018 he received the Jnanpith Award, the first writer in English to do so.

What makes these books feel Indian is the voice. Characters say "cousin-brother", eat "tiffin" and "prepone" a meeting. Rushdie mixed Hindi and Urdu words straight into his sentences without italics or explanation. Arundhati Roy played with capital letters and made up words, the way a child might.

Some readers find this hard at first. Others say it is simply how English sounds on the streets of Mumbai, Chennai or Kolkata. The novelist Raja Rao wrote in 1938 that "one has to convey in a language that is not one's own the spirit that is one's own", and generations of writers have tried.

Some writers grew up outside India. Jhumpa Lahiri, born in London to Bengali parents and raised in the USA, won the Pulitzer Prize in 2000 for *Interpreter of Maladies*. Her stories are about families who move between two countries, a feeling many in the [[@indian-diaspora|Indian diaspora]] know well.

There are also bestselling storytellers. [[@sudha-murty|Sudha Murty]]'s simple tales are loved by children and grandparents alike. Chetan Bhagat's novels about students sold in huge numbers, and several became Hindi films. Critics argue about which books are "literary", but readers decide for themselves.
